utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber will sit this morning in the absence of Judge Nosworthy, who's on other authorised Tribunal business. Mr. Shabani, the evidence will continue now. Please remember that the solemn declaration which you made at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Shabani.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, my name is John Ackerman. Along with Aleksanders Aleksic and Vujic, I'm representing General Pavkovic here. And I'm -- I've got several questions I want to ask you, and the quickest way for us to get through this is if you listen very carefully and only answer the question I ask you. As you know, the -- the basis of your account of what happened is already in the record in this case. The Judges have seen it, read it, heard it, they know about it, so it's not necessary you repeat things unless it's an answer to a specific question I ask you. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. The first thing I would like you to tell me is if you have learned from any source about testimony given in this case by other witnesses who appeared here before you did.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me about my own testimony? I gave it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you about if you've learned about testimony that was given in this case by other witnesses, who testified before you came here.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Everyone has his or her own testimony to give, and we have not talked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've not -- you've not watched or listened to any of these proceedings or read any news accounts, newspaper accounts or heard anything on the radio or TV? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have watched some of it on television, but I have not followed the testimony closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you say you've watched some of it on television, has that been on a local news channel of some kind?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I have watched it being mentioned on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2001, in June of 2001. And then you testified in the Milosevic case in March of 2002, and then you gave another statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, what is called a witness information -- addendum to the witness statement that you did on 27 August 2006. Correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to speak louder, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, the interpreters are asking you if you could speak a little louder so that they can hear exactly what you're saying. The microphone will be adjusted; that might be the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you met with the Prosecutors on 27 August 2006, you reviewed your earlier statement of 2001 and made several changes in it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I made some changes, because at that time there was another person who gave a statement but that witness was not summoned here to give evidence. So the evidence was not complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you gave your first statement, the one you gave back in June of 2001, according to the statement there was an interviewer and two interpreters present for that statement. And it took place over at least a three-day period. My question is this: When -- when that process was completed, that statement you gave was read back to you so you could be certain that it was correct, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was read back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was read back to you in such a way that you were able to -- to focus on what was being read to you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know, don't you, that you signed that statement?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know, don't you, that you signed an acknowledgement saying that it was read over to you in the Albanian language and was true to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you then came here in March of 2002 to give evidence in the Milosevic case, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, that's enough of the formality. Let's get to the point, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I'm getting there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's awfully slow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I believe it has to be, but I'll do my best to get to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You came to give evidence in the Milosevic case, and at that time you were -- you met with representatives of the Prosecutor, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you were asked to review your statement at that time and see if there were any changes you wished to make, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you gave your testimony in the Milosevic case, and that testimony was under oath, the same way as the testimony you're giving here today, was it not?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And my question now is why you didn't tell the Prosecutors when you were here in March of 2002 for the Milosevic case about the errors in your statement, since you'd then had two chances to review it.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I thought that the other person who gave his statement would also come here to give evidence and there was no need for me to make that supplement or changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you were content to have in existence a statement which you now say was not correct in many areas and that you've had to correct? You were content with that back in March of 2002. Is that what you're trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was content with it on the condition that the other person gave his own statement, because in this way both statements would cover everything that occurred in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. After you had testified in Milosevic, I assume that you received some kind of contact about the possibility of testifying in this case from the Prosecutor's office. Correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I came here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. Before you came here, you must have been contacted by the Office of the Prosecutor about the possibility that you would be testifying in this case, were you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they called me on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And my question now is: Were you ever told that it may be possible that your statement would just be used and that you would not have to come here? Were you ever told that?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not told that. They only asked me if I could come here to testify with respect to my statement. And then I said that: If you want me, I will come, and that's why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And during that telephone conversation, did you tell them that there were some errors in your statement that you would need to correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On that telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to now move to the early part of your account when you were in the village of Zhegra, your village. You told us in your statement that there were 97 Serb family homes in Zhegra. Correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately so. The number is not accurate. I didn't count them, but I think it's more or less accurate. I gave an approximate figure, as I said, because I didn't count the family homes. That's why I just made a guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what your statement says in paragraph 3 is -- there's no indication that it's a guess. You said: "There were also 97 Serb family homes here in the village." You didn't say "approximately" or "maybe" or anything like that, you just said that there were 97.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just mentioned the figure, but I may state here that I never counted them and that this figure was a supposition on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, anyone reading your statement without what you just said would be entitled to believe that there were exactly 97 Serb homes in that village, wouldn't they, because that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But as I said, being a villager, this is the number I thought they amounted to. But this is not a correct figure -- I mean an accurate figure I mean. Otherwise, had I counted them, I would certainly give you a very accurate figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know anybody when asked to estimate a number would come up with something like 97?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Impossible question --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- a precision like that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Impossible question for the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your statement you then said that these Serb families, 97 in your statement, "marked their homes by putting a piece of white cloth on the door," right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. This happened before that operation was undertaken to clean the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And now my question is this: Do you know - and I want to emphasise whether you know or not - do you know why those people put a piece of white cloth on their door? Not a guess, not a supposition, do you know why they did it?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because they wanted to be singled out from the Albanian homes. And this was the case in other villages, too, where there -- the population was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about other villages; I'm asking you about this village. And you know that because one of them told you that's why they put a white cloth on their door?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because other inhabitants told me this, but also because I've seen the white cloth with my own eyes, families living close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Whether you've seen it with your own eyes or not doesn't give you any indication of why it was there. What I want to know is: Did somebody tell you, one of those Serb families tell you, why they had put that cloth on the door? Is that how you know? Or are you just speculating again and guessing like you did with the 97 houses?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The Serbs told me why they put up that white cloth. But it was common knowledge that when the Serb forces came to clean the village, the military and paramilitary forces, entered only into the Albanian homes and not into the Serb homes. And that was clear to all of us why they put up that white cloth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if that was common knowledge and clear to everyone and everyone knew it and everyone knew why it was being put there, why didn't the Albanians just put white cloth on their houses, too, to protect themselves? Wouldn't that make sense?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. There were two Albanians who put up white cloths like the Serbs, but they were maltreated and insulted by the Serbian forces. This I didn't put in my statement, but I'm telling you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, these 97 Serb houses that -- or approximately 97, as you now say, that had this white cloth on them, did they all -- were they all in a line together facing the same direction?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were in different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did some of them face north?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some faced north, some faced south. As I said, the houses are scattered all over the village and the village is large. It's not a small one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did some face east and west?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. I don't understand your question. You mean the houses -- the Serb houses facing east or west or generally the houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were some of the Serb houses also facing east or west? You said they faced north and south. Did they also face east and west, some of them?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to understand this question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I didn't think it was difficult. I'm asking you about the Serb houses in your village that had white cloths on their front doors. Now, you already told me some of those houses faced to the north and some of them faced to the south. And the next question is, I think, easy: Did some of them also face to the east and the west?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the entrances to the yards of the houses? Because first you have to enter the yard, and they put this white cloth on the door or the gate of the house, not at the door, on the door of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. So in the statement when you said "door," that was another error and the white cloth was actually on the gate. So let's just ask the same question -- if you can do this quickly it would really please me. The gates of the Serb houses faced all directions, not just one. Correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We must understand each other. There is the house, there is a yard, and that's Serb property. At the gate or on the gate of that house, they put the white cloth. I want you to be clear what I mean. Not on the door of the house. First you have to pass the first gate of the yard, and then you enter the house through the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm now very clear about that. And that's not what I'm asking. And I think you know that's not what I'm asking. What I'm asking you is: Did those gates in front of those houses face more than one direction? Did they face all directions?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They faced different directions. It depends on the position, where it was built vis-a-vis the road or other points. There is the gate and then comes the house. So every Serbian household had such a white cloth put on the gate. I spoke in general, saying that every Serbian house was marked by a white cloth. I meant a house with a yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It took us way too long to get there. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I have to say, Mr. Ackerman, I don't know where the white cloth is now. I'm totally baffled. Is there only one gate or are there two gates? Because we have a reference to the first gate. Or is it on the gate at the street or where are we with these white cloths? And all you're tending to demonstrate is how difficult it is to note accurate statements from witnesses like this. And if this is the best inconsistency we've got, then I'm afraid, Mr. Ackerman, it's very peripheral to this man's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'm about to give up on this because I'm not going to get an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be good to get to something that matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would like to know, just to go back for a second, when was it you received a call from the OTP and you told them that there were errors in your statement? Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say there were errors, but I said I need to add some things regarding the question of the village, what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the question was: When was that phone call? That's what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That phone call was when they -- the Tribunal contacted me to come and testify here for the second time, here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, was that this year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you remember the month of the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was -- because I had to get ready, prepare the documents, get a new passport. It was the month of May, end of May I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you told them that you needed to add to your statement, were you asked what it was you needed to add?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, they didn't ask me anything. I told them that when I come there I will do what I need to do, and if you accept it, okay. This will depend on you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I now want to go to a different area. And this was the incident where a person named Avni was killed, and I'm referring now to your statement and I know that you have made what you call a correction in that. But, first of all, I want to refer just to your statement. And when I say "your statement," I mean your statement of 2001. Now, first of all -- the first thing you tell us in that statement that this incident happened a couple of days before the air-strikes, right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a mistake there. It was two or three days before the NATO air-strikes ended. This is when that incident occurred, that is in June. After I returned from Macedonia, I learned of that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so the first time you reviewed this statement you didn't notice that that was wrong, and the second time you reviewed the statement you didn't notice it was wrong. It was only the third time, after you'd come here for your testimony, that you take the position that that was wrong. Correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. But there is only one word, but it changes the whole meaning. It was something which escaped me when I first read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If what you're actually talking about is a couple of days before the air-strikes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I rise to object, Your Honour, belatedly. I think if it's going to be put to the witness that there was a mistake in the statement, then the proper context of this statement in respect to that incident should be put, and that is at paragraph 4 of the English statement. And since the witness is here, I just ask the Court to note the last sentence of that paragraph. So it's really a matter of how the statement is recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It could be paragraph 5 where it describes the incident in which Avni was killed, and in the last sentence he said: "I heard this from a local after I returned." It could be well how you interpret that sentence, because he's being told now that it was only later, much later, that he indicated that he discovered this in June when that is not necessarily the appropriate interpretation of the meaning of that sentence in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We reject that proposition. The statement is abundantly clear, and the only thing that might be in doubt is the extent to which he claims to have heard it from a local after he returned, but there's no doubt that he said in the statement "a couple of days before the air-strikes a man from this village ..." Carry on, Mr. Ackerman. Let's bring common sense to bear on these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what you said at that time in the statement that you reviewed and approved on at least two occasions -- well, let me ask you a preliminary question. You were in the village at home two days before the NATO bombing started, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then what you say after that first phrase about when this happened, you say that: "Avni was walking to his home, which is situated behind my house and higher up on the hill. It was in the evening time. There was about three or four policemen I knew in the field about 400 metres from him. One was called Jova, another was Dragan, the others I did not know. The two I have named were from Zhegra." Then you go on: "From a distance they shot at Avni and then they went and mutilated the body. I don't know why they did this, though." Now, one could get the impression -- I haven't asked you a question --

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, after I returned from Presheva --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Wait until you're asked a question. Carry on, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One could get the impression from that that you were there and that you were an eye-witness to this event because it's described in such detail about where it was in relation to your house, what time it was in the evening, the policemen that you knew and recognised. I mean, anyone who would read that and think you were reporting was someone told you is not reading correctly, right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is narrated as if I've seen it with my own eyes. That's how persons who told me this narrated it because they were with Avni until they separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Who was the person who told you about this after you returned, which you now say was how it happened?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My neighbour Hisen Hiseni and his brother Idriz Hiseni. They live close to my house, and when we met they told me what had happened and that's what I described here in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I now submit to you that that can't possibly be true because you told us that it was Hisen Hiseni who gave you the other story about what happened there. It is not this story.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is exactly this story, not another story. I haven't mentioned his name with reference to other stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we're going to get to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's not lose sight of it at the moment. Where do you say that is? Just give me a paragraph number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's page 1572 of the Milosevic statement -- of the Milosevic trial. And I'll just go to it right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At page 1572 in the Milosevic trial, Mr. Milosevic asked you the following question: "You said that the army shot at a person called Avni, that they killed him. As a matter of fact, you said that they massacred him, and the truth is quite different. This person was retarded. The army found him dead and brought him there, and that's where the authorities got this statement from the father, that this is a young man who was mentally retarded whom they had tied up themselves so that he would not create problems for them. Do you know about that?" And you gave this answer: "Yes. I have heard about this case when I returned, that Mr. Zenani was killed by Serbian civilians of the Zhegra village who were armed. Those civilians were armed and the killing was carried out on the 6th of June" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: July, I think. That must be a misprint. My copy --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It later gets corrected that it was June instead of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, that's a totally different story than the one that was in your statement to the OTP, that he was killed by these police officers that you knew, that he was shot by them, and you agreed with Mr. Milosevic, that what he had suggested to you was true. So did Hiseni tell you two stories?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the killing of Shukri Isufi's son, I heard about it from his father, from Shukri himself. And during the Milosevic trial I mentioned that this killing was carried out by Serb paramilitaries who entered by force his compound. His father was also there present, but in hiding. He was hiding. When the killing took place, he was covered with hay and he did not dare come out of the haystack. So he was hiding there in the haystack. This is what I discussed with Milosevic during that trial at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I'm not understanding your point that he agreed in the evidence in Milosevic with the proposition. The proposition was that his own family had tied him up and left him to die.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, and after Milosevic had made this statement he said: Do you know about that? And the witness said: "Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But he goes on to say Mr. Zenani was killed by Serbian civilians of the Zhegra village who were armed and the killing was carried out on the 6th of June to intimidate the Albanian population. That's not agreeing with his version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm really not suggesting that he agreed with it was done by his father who tied him up and so forth. And even if it was tied up by his father, he still could have been killed by Serb civilians. In any event, it doesn't have an any effect on where I'm trying to go with this. Where I'm going with this is, is he's telling two completely different stories. One, he's killed by Serb civilians on the 6th of June; another is he's killed by police that he knows personally a couple of days before the air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. I now understand the point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you've now told a third account, haven't you, a third version of this story, when you talked to the Prosecutor on 27 August 2006. Correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, sir, Your Honours, you are not referring to this correctly. You have mixed things up with other persons. I don't know to which incident you are referring specifically. If, for example, we are speaking of Avni Zenani, this is a person I've mentioned earlier, and in the additional statement I said on basis of what I heard, he was killed on the 6th of June around 1700 hours and that he was taken to Gjilan morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please don't, we don't need the whole story. We're talking about the same person. Every incident I've talked about is the same person. Mr. Milosevic talked about Avni. Your statement to the OTP in 2001 talks about Avni. And finally, when you talked to the Prosecutor here, you tell the Prosecutor his last name was Zenani. But in your -- your contention in Milosevic and your contention so far today in this case was that you learned about this incident after you returned. Now, that's not the same thing you told the Prosecutor on August 27th. What you told the Prosecutor then was, in paragraph 6: "I heard about this incident from another person while I was in Macedonia." Now, is it true that you're just making this all up and not getting the story straight?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm telling the truth. That's why I'm here, but it is difficult for the truth to come on to surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, it sure is when you tell three stories. It's very difficult for us to know which one is the truth, if any, and I suggest to you perhaps none of them are.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I've said so far is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you've said three different things. How could they all be true?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, this is where we descend, really, to the point where there is nothing productive that emerges. Having made your point, can you not settle for it and move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I settle for it, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you tell us how far your village of Zhegra is from the Macedonian border?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, about 30 kilometres, approximately. I haven't measured the distance. It could be more or even less. So that's why I'm saying it's just an approximate figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After the -- the Serb forces, the Serb soldiers, whoever they were, came to your village and started staying there and digging trenches and doing things like that, did you know about some killings that occurred and I want to ask you about the killings of - and I may badly mispronounce these names - Qamil Idrizi, Milazim and Shyqri Tahiri? Do you know about the killing of any those people?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And I have testified to that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you also know that a Serb by the name of Vlada Zmajevic and six additional VJ volunteers were arrested by VJ security and turned over to the Pristina Corps court for trial for those murders?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've not heard about that?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it, then, you don't know that these seven individuals are currently serving prison sentences, having been convicted of these murders?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I don't know that they have been sentenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, where do we find that in the statements or the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't find it anywhere or any place, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is a reference to a name Tahiri, but that's different, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, you won't find these anywhere in the transcripts, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But I have a good-faith basis for asking these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you see, the witness says he's testified to the event and that's why I thought we might have something on it. But you say that's wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it may be that in the Milosevic transcript he talked about it or -- I don't know where it is in his statement that he talked about these particular individuals being killed. He may have testified to it in Milosevic, I just don't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have mentioned them in the supplement statement that I gave, in the addendum, not during the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know that the -- the investigation of the incidents that happened in your village is still going on by the Belgrade Special Court? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I have no knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know or have you heard that a couple of Serb civilians in Zagreb [sic] by the name of Zvonimir Pavic and Milan Jovanovic were arrested for robbing the house of one Rexhep Ajati in Vitia? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at line 24 the transcript says "Zagreb" and it should say "Zhegra."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you know about the rest of Marinkovic and Denic from Perlepnica arrested by SUP and VJ security for setting fire to a number of houses? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I haven't heard about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to now go to the time you spent in Stubla. You left the village of Zhegra with your family on 29 March 1999, and you went toward Donja Stubla. Correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And tell us just briefly why it is you left the village on the 29th of March?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we feared that we would be executed by the Serb forces who had already started killing people in the village, like they killed Shyqri Tahiri, the brother of Tahir Tahiri, and they had started to shell with artillery weapons. I have mentioned a transporter in the village. And not only me but the entire village fled in the direction of Kushtavice [phoen], where we thought we would be safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, so you spent the night up there on Kuslevica mountain in the rain, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, together with other people from Zhegra.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There were about 1200 of you there; correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, yes. Not all of them that I knew, but it was just a mass of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. And of that approximate number of 1200, would you hazard a guess as to how many of those were men between 16 and 60 years old?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't counted them. There were men, women, children --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just say you don't know and that ends it. So then the next morning you went back to this village where you feared that you would be executed by the Serb forces who had already started killing people in the village, like they killed Mr. Tahiri, the brother of Tahir Tahiri, where they had started to shell with artillery weapons. Correct? You went back to that village that you said you left yesterday because of all these fears, the day before?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we went back because we thought that their activity have ceased and that the situation would become calmer. That's why we went back to the village. And only those villagers who lived in and around the centre of the village, like more inside the village, they returned. And they then moved in the peripheral parts in case of sudden attacks by the Serb forces, which actually happened. There was firing on all sides, from all sides. You could hear machine-gun fire --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb forces, paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've testified about this and I didn't ask you about that. What was it, as you were spending the night up on this mountain in the rain that caused you to believe that the activity had ceased and the situation had become calmer? What led you to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we could no longer hear shots firing, and we could no longer see their movements. This is why -- this is how we saw it. We thought that they were not going to touch us. But on the contrary, the biggest incidents occurred then, like the case with Ukshin Ukshini and his wife, Milazim Idrizi --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're trying to move along as fast as we can. You don't need to tell us things twice; I told you that this morning. Now, the other thing I wanted to ask you about that. You could see this village from the mountain where you were spending the night in the rain and determine whether there were movements in the village or not?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could see movement but not from the centre -- central part of the village. The Serb forces were in the building of the primary school, and in the agricultural co-operative and the factory as well as in some Albanian houses in the vicinity of the factory. These are the locations where the Serb forces were positioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: While they were there, those forces were digging trenches and setting up a defensive line, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they dug trenches only in those places where they thought they would face NATO forces. But they were positioned in Zhegra. This was during the bombing and before the bombing. On the 29th and 30th of March --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We already know about that. You've told us about that. I want to ask you -- now, you came back down from the mountain to the village. Did you spend that night in the village after you came back or did you leave that very same day?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we spent the night in the village with family members and with other villagers who had their houses in the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so it was the next day, then, that you left and went to Donja Stubla, where you stayed for five weeks. Correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So on the 30th we set off after we were expelled by the paramilitary forces and Serbian military forces. They were shooting from all sides and expelling people from their houses, killing them, injuring them, beating them up. So we fled in the direction of Stublla i Ulet. The entire village fled in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember -- excuse me. Do you remember the question that I asked you? Do you remember what I asked you? Could you tell me the question that I asked you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me if you went to Stublla village on the 30th? And I explained to you that we did, and I explained how we went to Stublla.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is there any reason you couldn't have just said: Yes, that's the day we went to Stublla, because that's what I asked you, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've discussed this problem before, Mr. Ackerman. These questions are actually unnecessary, and they do tend to encourage witnesses who come from this region to answer in the way in which this witness answered. It is far from exclusive to him. So we've all got to learn as we go along that we're dealing with people from different culture, different jurisdictions who perceive questions differently, and we've got to tailor our questions to try and avoid these problems. I don't think it's fair to blame the witness for that. But I'm happy to intervene a bit more, if that's what you want me to do to stop the answers, but I think it then becomes rather unfortunate. So the best way to deal with this is to try and avoid the questions that don't really matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the question matters, Your Honour, because it's not clear from anything he's put in his statement or said whether they spent the night in that village and left the next day or not. That's what I was trying to figure out, is this village that was so dangerous they went back to and spent the whole night in before they left again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's where I was going and I was just trying to lead to where I was going next.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I've not asked a question. Please don't answer anything. I didn't ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just wait, Mr. Shabani, until you're asked a question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There were no KLA in Donja Stubla, were there?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And during the entire five weeks you were there, there was no KLA there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. There was no KLA forces in Gjilan or in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And because there was no KLA there, then the Serbian forces had no interest in coming into that village and in fact didn't come into that village. Correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why they didn't enter. I don't know what purposes they had. I know only that there was no KLA and that civilian population was there in -- spread out in different houses and in nylon tents when they didn't have a shelter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Shabani. We've got enough of the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you said also that about 500 to a thousand people a day left Donja Stubla and went to Macedonia. And you tell us in your statement that they left because of, and these are your words, "fear and because they did not have any food." Correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Out of fear, because even as it is they had been displaced from their homes, from Zhegra and from other villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And my question now is this: If they had had no fear, if there'd been nothing for them to be afraid of, they still would have left because they had no food. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this a serious question, Mr. Ackerman? We're not dealing with a jury here, as I've said repeatedly. That's a -- a pointless question in the context of the trial we are conducting. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I thought it went to a pretty important issue in the trial, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we disagree with you. Well, at least we disagree that the question will help us to reach an answer to what I do agree with you is a very important issue in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's different. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us in your statement - you changed this in your new statement to the OTP - but in your old statement you said, and let me find it, in paragraph 18, the statement that you reviewed twice and swore was correct: "During the five weeks we were in Stublla, we had a normal life." You've told us now in your new statement to the OTP that it's not true, that you didn't have a normal life, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the entire statement, you will understand that there was no normal life. That was a way of speaking, of saying, you know -- because if you look at my statement you will see that there was no normal life. We were constantly in fear and on the watch-out less we were killed or attacked by the Serbian forces at day or at night and ready to leave if they did so. So that cannot be a normal life. I don't know if you agree with me, but that's how I saw it and see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said you were keeping guard at night. What kind of weapons did the people have that were keeping guard at night, if any?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any weapons. We just kept vigil to be prepared and not be caught asleep if they attacked us in case of some bloodshed that might occur, that we feared. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. So finally then on the 2nd of May of 1999 you decided to leave Stublla, along with about 600 people. Now, who made the decision, among that 600, who decided to leave?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a spontaneous decision. Every family was eager to flee in that event, so everybody was interested in finding a way to find a safer place. Because we didn't know what the morrow might bring to us. So every family made up its own mind, and this is how we came together, spontaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you hadn't known what the morrow might bring to you for five weeks, and then all of a sudden one morning you say spontaneously 600 people said: Okay, we're leaving. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other groups before us who left. I told you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's clearly not my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, the question is: What was it that made you think after five weeks of nothing happening at all that you were still in danger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the constant danger facing us. As I said, we did not know what the morrow might bring. We were living in constant fear. We knew that the Serbian forces would one day come to the village, and we were afraid they would kill each and every one of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you stayed there -- you stayed there for five weeks. Now, what was it that triggered the move? Why after five weeks did you decide to move on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because we saw that the situation was not improving, the houses were set on fire, and there was no turn back for us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What point was it -- you mean -- sorry, when were the houses set on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the population left the village of Zhegra from the 6th of April, 10 and 15 houses kept burning constantly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Nothing happened in Donja Stubla on the day before you left or the night before you left, no shots were fired at that village, no Serb forces came to that village. It was the same as it had been for the preceding days. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Stublla, yes, but around it, no. And in other villages, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we followed what was going on in village -- in other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you're satisfied to leave this Chamber with the proposition that for no good reason on one morning 600 people just got up and said: Let's leave, I'm satisfied with that, too. Are you satisfied with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's arguing with the witness, Your Honour. The witness has answered this question many times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go now into your trip to Macedonia. At page 1535 in the Milosevic testimony, talking about that trip you said: "We moved at night because we didn't want to be discovered by Serbian forces." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were always careful not to run into Serbian forces when we walked at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's why you moved at night, was to avoid Serbian forces. Isn't that what you were saying in Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I said in Milosevic trial but also in my statement, that we walked at night, trying to move as cautiously as we could so that we didn't suffer any consequences from the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you spent a night in a village called Seferaj, yeah?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It was there that we spent the night after we passed Jsufaj village, Rekaj, the river in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Next morning you left there and went to Rustaje where you arrived around 2.00 in the afternoon. So in that instance you travelled in the day-time?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But always keeping to the hills and avoiding the main roads where the Serbian forces were moving. So we tried to find secondary and tertiary roads, if I might say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, when you got to Rustaje, you encountered some forces there, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And these forces had set up defensive positions in the area of Rustaje, had they not?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had taken up positions there, and when they saw us they surrounded us and took us to the place where they wanted us to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And they searched you to make sure that you had no weapons, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They searched us -- everything we had on us, our documents and everything. It was a very detailed search, both men and women.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And then they escorted you to a hill near the border, and at that point told you to go to Presevo, right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you are not mentioning everything that I said in my statement. They first surrounded us. We stayed out in the rain for two hours and a half and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... told us all about that in your statement and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, we don't need to go over your statement again. We just need answers to specific questions, please. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, after you were escorted to this hill, these soldiers told you to go to Presevo and escorted you no further. You were on your own at that point, after being told to go to Presevo. Correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They did not escort us. They just showed us direction to go, and we set out in that direction. But we turned back --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, we know that, too. And Presevo -- Presevo is in Serbia, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So these soldiers were telling you that you should go to Serbia, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They sent some other groups before us in the direction of Presheva --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it might be to your advantage if you just listen to the rest of the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, instead of going to Presevo you went a different way and went to Macedonia, and on the way I think you say you spent another night in a place called Mal i Thate, I'll pronounce that wrong, but Mal i Thate? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you joined about 300 other civilians there with your group, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had gone from Presheva in the direction of Mal i Thate and they joined us. There were villagers from my village in that group as well, and we spent the night in Mal i Thate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that group that was around 900 people now were all Kosovo Albanians, were they?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all of us were Albanians of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some from Presheva, but there were very few, maybe one or two. The bulk of us were Albanians from Kosova. And from the same area, we set out from Stublla.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And one of these Albanians you said knew the way to the border crossing and showed you the way?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One Albanian from Presheva, he told us that he knew the way and that maybe he had connections with the Serbian forces and that he showed us the way to cross the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You just said it again, but you said in Milosevic pretty much the same thing: "This person who was certainly urged by the Serbian forces, asked us ... to give him some ... Deutschmarks ... to show us the place. I think everything was done in collaboration with the Serbian forces, the border forces." Are you just guessing about that or do you know that this person was collaborating with Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they took from every one of us 10 Deutschmarks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, let's concentrate on the question. What makes you think that this person was associated with Serbian forces? What's the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His words, what he told us. He told us that: I have to pay -- to give this money I'm collecting from you to the Serbian forces at the border. This is what made me think or all of us think that he was associated with the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Serbian forces that you'd encountered were trying to get you to go to Serbia. So if he was associated with the Serbian forces, why didn't he take you to Serbia instead of Macedonia? I'm sure you don't know the answer to that. You can just say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- I don't understand your question, sir. If you can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't want to ask it. I do want to ask you this: When you actually finally got to the border, near the border you saw some more Serb soldiers in trenches guarding the border and they didn't bother you in any way. Correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They were in their positions, and we didn't hear anything -- them say anything to us or didn't hear any fire shot. We were in a column, and this is how we crossed the border in an Indian file because this is what they told us that the border was mined and that we had to be very careful while we moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So at -- at best, they seemed to be concerned for your safety and told you to be very careful and avoid the mines, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that was their intention --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- go to another subject completely. At page 1.525 of the Milosevic transcript, you were talking about the beginning of the NATO bombing and you said it made the Serbs very angry. And then you said this: "Certain people had made certain preparations under orders from Belgrade." Now, first of all, what certain people had made these preparations? Who were you talking about there that had made these preparations?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, under orders from Belgrade the local inhabitants had made preparations to launch the operation for cleansing the village and eliminating certain people. They had taken care to get -- to be ready for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it was the local Serb villagers who were doing this cleansing. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local Serbs, together with the Serbian forces that were stationed in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you say this had something to do with an order from Belgrade. When did you see that order and where did you see it?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the order. They must have seen it, but I presume that they organised themselves on the basis of orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So this was just a presumption when you said it had -- was based on an order from Belgrade, you were just presuming that, guessing that. True?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every action that is undertaken normally is undertaken on some orders coming from above.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the answer is: Yes, you were just presuming and guessing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, at page 1527 of that transcript you were asked if there were any skirmishes between residents of your village and the Serb forces, and you said there weren't any because: "We didn't have any weapons." Now, nobody in your village had any weapons?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any weapons. If someone had a weapon, a pistol or some other weapon, he had no chance of using it against an armoured car or a tank, even if they had such kind of weapon. Normally they had them, they would hide the weapon and not use it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know that no one had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, why are you telling us what people would do with weapons if they had them if nobody had a weapon. What was the point in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to -- my point was that even if they had a pistol, they wouldn't dare to use it, because if an Albanian killed a single Serb the retaliation would be huge. This is my point when saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can't you understand all we want to know is whether or not anyone had any weapons? That's all the question was about, not what they would have done with them if they had them. Please confine your answers to the questions you're actually asked, and we'll get to the end of this eventually if we do that. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, they didn't have weapons, at least most of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Instead of giving a simple clear answer, you've left us wondering: Well, did some people have weapons and were they hiding them because of the answer you've given. It's not helpful to us. It's certainly not helpful to you if in fact the truth of the matter is that nobody had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps now is a suitable time to break, although I hope we're making some progress through this cross-examination, Mr. -- how long are we going to be with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know what anyone else is going to do. I'm going to be another five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll break now and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before we resume, I just wanted to indicate we had a new member of our team sitting in today. This is Yana Mihaylova who is an intern working with us on the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Shabani, I gather from the court deputy that you want to correct something from the evidence you gave yesterday. What is it you wish to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the uniforms worn by Serb forces in the village and regarding the APC that was firing at the village, I just wanted to define these two issues in a clearer way. So I was just asking for an opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if anyone wishes to ask you more questions about that, they will have the opportunity to do so and you can deal with it at that stage. Meanwhile, we're carry on with the questions. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to refer now to the time you went back to your village, to Zhegra. Was that after -- that was after the NATO forces had come into Kosovo. Correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned from Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. After the NATO forces entered Kosova, on the 24th of June, 1999, I returned to Zhegra village, to Kosova, with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so after the Serb forces left and the NATO forces came, what happened in your village was that all the Serb houses were burned to the ground and the Orthodox church was burned to the ground. Correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was like a retaliation for what the Serbs had previously done to Albanian properties. In other words, as the Serbs burned the mosque and Albanian houses, some Albanians, when they returned, they set Serbian houses on fire after the Serbs had left their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you assist in that in any way? Did you do any burning or anything?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not participate in any way, and it took me by surprise as well. To my opinion -- in my opinion, I don't think they should have been set on fire. They should have been left there untouched for the Serbs to be able to return to their houses as well. This is my opinion, and I stick to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you were talking in the Milosevic case about the pieces of white cloth that the Serbs put on their -- now you say their gates, you said this: "These white cloths resembled a fascist genocide." What does that mean? What do you mean they resembled a fascist genocide?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hatred and to divide one nation from another and exterminate the other nation by using weapons, how else can you define this but as a fascist genocide, the killings, the fire that was carried out in the village by Serb paramilitary forces and army?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So would you characterise the KLA, who were killing Serb police and killing Albanian civilians in the same way, that they were engaged in a fascist genocide?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The KLA did not kill Serb policemen just like that. It fought in front lines. They were waging a liberation war. As I said, there were no KLA in Zhegra, but in those areas of Kosova where the KLA was present, they were fighting for Kosova's liberation from the Serb forces and police as well as the paramilitary forces that were at that time in Kosova. And with the help of NATO as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you about something you said regarding the KLA in Milosevic. It's page 1578. You were asked about your views regarding the KLA and you said this: "In my view, the KLA is not a terrorist organisation but an organisation that stood up in defence of the people and fought the Serb terror and atrocities perpetrated against the Albanian population of Kosovo." Mr. Milosevic then asked you this: "If they fought against Serb terror, why then did they kill so many Albanians?" And you said this: "If they've killed Albanians who've been involved and cooperated with the Serb forces, that is, traitors to the nation, they may have done such a thing." Traitors to what nation would these people be? What nation would they be traitors to?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, an Albanian who collaborating with Serbian forces; this is what I mean, who was a collaborator and who was detected in these activities by the KLA, he was liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What nation was that person being a traitor to? What nation was it for him to be a traitor to, to commit treason against? Certainly not Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I say "a traitor to a nation," I mean the Albanian nation, a person who served the Serbian police and army, who aided and abetted them in carrying out these massacres of the Albanian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So he was a traitor of the country of Albania, which is next to Serbia? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Traitor to the Albanian interest of the Albanians in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But that was not a nation, was it? That was part of Serbia. So he was supporting the Serbian forces trying to put down a rebellion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is unproductive now, Mr. Ackerman. You've dealt long enough with this subject. And we have the transcript as well which goes into it in some detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: You told us about a person when you were crossing the border into Macedonia, an Albanian person, who you said was working with the Serb forces and taking money from you. Would you consider that person a traitor who probably should have been killed?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Exactly what I asked you. Would you consider that person a traitor? If he was collaborating with Serb forces when he took you cross the border. Is he a traitor who should have been killed by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying that he should have been killed by the KLA, but if he is of that kind and is a citizen of Kosova, if he cooperated and collaborated with Serbian forces and harmed the Albanians of Kosova, he should be held responsible for these deeds through courts. This is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And would that also be your opinion if someone from your village would come here and testify in front of this Trial Chamber that some of the things you've told us today were not true, would you consider that person a traitor also?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's -- that's a question that is not appropriate for the witness. It's -- in fact, it's argumentative, Mr. Ackerman, and we've had enough of that in this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm finished, Your Honour. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac -- Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Shabani. My name is Djuro Cepic, one of the counsel for General Vladimir Lazarevic. I have in my hand a map of the area, including the village of Zegra. When I look at it, I conclude that Zegra is but a few kilometres away from the border with Macedonia. Is that correct? I'm talking about the distance as the crow flies, being the shortest distance.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told the Court that I did not measure the distance. We are speaking of the place where I come from. If you're speaking about the location where I was, near the border, then it's a shorter distance. But Zhegra is further. I don't understand your question. I don't understand the purpose of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It is not for you to assess the purpose of my question, but rather to answer it. And I believe my answer [as interpreted] was a clear one. As the crow flies, can we say that Zegra, the village of Zegra, is not far from the state border with Macedonia, taking the shortest distance?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as the crow flies or the actual distance, it's not very far. As I said, it's about 30 kilometres. But again, I'm telling you I didn't measure the distance and I cannot give you the exact estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, I didn't ask you about any roads. I asked you about the distance as the crow flies. You have been asked about the roads by Mr. Ackerman. I have this map in front of me, so I put it to you that it is as I stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why don't you put the distance that you say it is and get an answer to that? You should have prepared the cross-examination so you know the distance. So you should be able to put that to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Approximately four to five kilometres as the crow flies, being the shortest distance to reach the Macedonian border.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true. It can't be true, four or five kilometres. It's definitely further, even as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that along the Macedonian border in that area, being to the south of the village of Zegra, there were post -- border posts by the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the south of the village of Zhegra, well, the road that -- along the road from Zhegra to the Macedonian border, there were Serbian check-points and trenches used by the police --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Used by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, could you please provide specific answers to what I believe are specific questions. I asked you about the border posts of the Army of Yugoslavia south of Zegra on the border with Macedonia. I didn't ask you about any check-points.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are not speaking of the police, but about the Serbian army and other paramilitaries that were along the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, is it accurate to say that the police controlled -- that the army controlled the border crossings? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It controlled the state boundary. I had in mind the control of the state boundary. I didn't have in mind the state crossing -- the border crossings; I had in mind the posts, the blockhouses, towerhouses, on the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do you know about these, Mr. Shabani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I learned from some villagers that certain villages that were on the border between Serbia and Macedonia, the inhabitants of these border villages were expelled and moved to Zhegra --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not the question you're being asked. Now, I have to wonder what you're trying to do when you give an answer like that. The question is whether you know about army posts located on the Macedonian border.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've only seen trenches along the road. I don't know of any other guard posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, I didn't ask you about the route you travelled; I asked you about something else, but let us move on. Did you know that there were illegal crossings of the border before NATO bombing began and that the Army of Yugoslavia would having caught those people who tried to cross the border illegally without papers, they turned them over to the investigative bodies of the state, and this was all verified by the OSCE mission that was in the field at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's no way the witness will know the answer to that question. What is the relevance of this line of cross-examination to this witness's evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, having in mind the answers I received, I was about to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me it's been an utter waste of time so far, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, did you know that members of the Ministry of the Interior in the village of -- from the village of Gnjilane, having come to the village of Zegra on the 27th of January, 1999, detained Mustafaj Bekim, who was born in 1975, and his brother Lulzim. They detained these two Albanians because of an attack they allegedly carried out against another Albanian, Ibrahim Salihu?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about this case. And I don't even know the names of the persons you mentioned. No, I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you know that on the 16th of February, 1999, in the same village of Zegra, members of the police seized two pieces of weapons from a local Albanian by the name of Agushi Muhamed?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about this either.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
